newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Miss World protests not what they used to be.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Miss World protests not what they used to be.

text.p: Miss World organiser Julia Morley, whose beauty pageant in India is haunted by suicide threats from protesters, reminisced to Reuters about the days of the womens' liberation movement in the 1970s.
Back then no-one ever really got hurt.
"Someone once stubbed a cigarette out on the back of a policeman's hand," she said, sitting in a Bangalore hotel where the Miss World bandwagon is staying, guarded by hundreds of police.
Last week an Indian man sent shudders through the Miss World camp by burning himself to death to protest against the show which opponents say offends women and Indian culture.
"I can't accept (it) when someone wants to kill themselves or harm others to protest," the Miss World Limited international president told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday night.

In the past, demonstrations against the contest sometimes caused chaos, but were never really threatening -- discounting a lone incident in the early 1970s when a British activist group, the Angry Brigade, planted a bomb near a television production van.
The protests even had a farcical side, Morley said, thinking of the night she clung to American comedian Bob Hope's ankles to stop him fleeing the stage.
Miss World will be crowned in Bangalore on Saturday in front of an estimated television audience of two billion.
At the same time Kina Narayana Shashikala, and some of her followers in the Mahila Jagran Samiti (Forum for Awakening Women), have threatened multiple self immolation.
Police plan to deploy 12,000 officers on the final night, who will be backed by paramilitary officers, due to the threats of multiple suicides.
Shashikala's rhetoric is aimed against exploitation of women and contamination of Indian culture with western values.
"If she's genuine she should come and form a dialogue with us to understand that we are interested in some of the same problems," Morley said.
Morley said participants in the feminist movement in the 1970s also refused to talk and used the show to promote their cause, but she subsequently formed a dialogue with the activists.
"They admitted Miss World was a useful tool to air their views and that they went to extremes to get those views across."
She laughed, recalling the pandemonium at a show at the Royal Albert Hall in London in the late 1970s, when Bob Hope was the star attraction.

"Protestors were running around, not just women but drag queens (men in womens' clothes), old ladies in the audience were hitting them with handbags and policemen were chasing them. There were smoke bombs going off."
"And I was holding onto Bob Hope's ankles saying you've got to stay on."
So would Morley stage Miss World in India again?
"I'm not a glutton for punishment. But yes, I would come back if this young woman doesn't kill herself and I could do the show well."
